claims.text: An ultrathin Ag-rich layer can be introduced at the interface between tungsten and copper phases.
The Ag-rich interfacial layer will reduce W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance.
Reducing interfacial thermal resistance will increase the effective thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
The Ag-modified W–Cu composite will retain mechanical durability.
The Ag-modified W–Cu composite will retain resistance to irradiation-induced damage.
W–Cu composites with untreated W–Cu interfaces are used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
Fusion-reactor components can operate at temperatures of at least 1000 K under intense particle and neutron exposure.
Fusion applications require materials to maintain mechanical integrity while removing severe heat loads under irradiation.
The deposited Ag will form a coherent or semi-coherent Ag-enriched interfacial phase between W and Cu grains.
The Ag-enriched phase will bridge the structural mismatch between W and Cu grains.
The Ag-enriched interface will enhance phonon and electron transport across the W–Cu interface.
Silver has inherently high thermal conductivity.
An Ag transitional layer will minimize lattice mismatch and interfacial defects at the W–Cu interface.
A continuous Ag layer will preserve overall composite microstructural integrity.
Preservation of microstructural integrity by the Ag layer will maintain mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
Relative to an untreated control, the Ag-interlayer composite will have measurably higher effective thermal conductivity and similar or only marginally altered strength and radiation tolerance.
The benefit depends on the Ag layer remaining stable without excessive diffusion or phase degradation at operating temperature and radiation dose.
An excessively thick or poorly bonded Ag interlayer may compromise mechanical integrity.
The optimal Ag-layer thickness, uniformity, irradiation stability, and long-term interdiffusion behavior remain experimentally undetermined.
